name: B1 — Intermediate
description: Subjunctive, conditional, ser vs estar, por vs para, double object pronouns — the structural backbone of intermediate Spanish.

topics.title: Present Perfect — he/has + participio
topics.description: Past events with present relevance (he comido, has visto)

guide.intro: Spanish present perfect is formed with HABER + past participle: 'he comido' (I have eaten). It looks just like English, but usage differs by region. In Spain, 'he comido pizza esta semana' is normal. In Latin America, you'll often hear preterite — 'comí pizza esta semana' — for the same idea.

sections.text: Two confusions: (1) Spanish 'he' is unrelated to English 'he' — it means 'I have'. (2) The participle never changes — always 'comido', never 'comida' even with feminine subjects: 'María ha comido' not 'María ha comida'.
Use it for: (a) life experiences (¿Has estado en México?), (b) actions in time periods still open (hoy, esta semana), (c) actions with present consequence (he perdido las llaves).

rows.source: Esta mañana he ido al gimnasio.
rows.translation: This morning I went to the gym.

sections.text: Spain uses present perfect liberally for anything today or recent. Latin America strongly prefers preterite. 'Hoy he ido al banco' (Spain) vs 'Hoy fui al banco' (LatAm) — same idea.
Time markers: ya (already), todavía no / aún no (not yet), nunca (never), alguna vez (ever), siempre (always), hoy (today), esta semana/mes/año, últimamente (lately).

topics.title: Present Subjunctive — the WEIRDO triggers
topics.description: Wishes, emotions, doubt, recommendations — the mood with no clean English equivalent

guide.intro: The subjunctive is THE B1 milestone. English barely uses it ('if I were you'); Spanish uses it constantly. Endings are a small set — the hard part is knowing WHEN. The trigger is in the FIRST clause: something subjective pushes the verb in the 'que' clause into the subjunctive.

rows: querer que, esperar que, desear que
me alegra que, me molesta que, me da pena que
es importante que, es necesario que, es bueno que
recomendar que, pedir que, sugerir que
no creo que, dudar que, no es verdad que

sections.text: Take the YO form of present indicative, drop -o, add 'opposite' vowel endings: -ar verbs take -e endings, -er/-ir verbs take -a endings.
The clue 'que' is your friend. Structure: [Main clause with subjective trigger] + QUE + [different subject + subjunctive]. Same subject? Use infinitive instead.

rows.translation: I want to eat. (same subject → infinitive)
I want YOU to eat. (different subject → subjunctive)

rows.source: Espero que tengas un buen día.
rows.translation: I hope you have a good day.

sections.text: When you KNOW something is true, stay in indicative. When you express doubt, hope, emotion, or a wish about it, switch to subjunctive. 'Sé que viene' (fact) vs 'Espero que venga' (wish).

topics.title: The Conditional — 'would' in Spanish
topics.description: haría, comería, viviría — hypothetical and polite forms

guide.intro: Spanish has a clean, single-word conditional. Where English uses 'would + verb', Spanish glues -ía onto the infinitive. Two main jobs: (1) hypothetical situations and (2) softening for politeness ('could you?', 'would you mind?').

sections.text: Take the WHOLE infinitive (don't drop -ar/-er/-ir) and add conditional endings. Same endings for all three conjugations.

rows.translation: If I had money, I would travel.

sections.text: Conditional is built-in polite. 'Quiero un café' (blunt) → 'Querría un café' / 'Me gustaría un café' (polite restaurant version).
Don't confuse conditional ('vendría' — would come) with imperfect ('venía' — used to come). Conditional always has -ría- somewhere.

topics.title: Ser vs Estar — meaning shifts
topics.description: Beyond A1: when the SAME adjective changes meaning

guide.intro: By B1 you know ser = essence, estar = state/location. The advanced twist: many adjectives have TWO meanings — one with ser, another with estar. 'Es aburrido' (boring/dull) vs 'Está aburrido' (bored right now). Classic English-speaker trap.

rows.translation: My teacher is boring (a dull person).
I'm bored. Want to go to a movie?
Are you ready? We leave in 5.

sections.text: Even outside dual-meaning adjectives, ser vs estar carries nuance. 'Es delgado' (he is thin — description). 'Está delgado' (he LOOKS thin — has lost weight). Estar often expresses 'looks/seems' or 'has become'.
Estar muerto/vivo: dead and alive both use ESTAR, even though death is permanent! Spanish treats them as states resulting from a change. 'Mi abuelo está muerto.'
Rule of thumb: 'feel/look/seem' → ESTAR. Unchanging classification → SER. Permanent label or current state?

options: My uncle is boring (a dull person)

topics.title: Por vs Para — both mean 'for'
topics.description: POR = cause, duration, exchange, motion-through. PARA = purpose, destination, deadline, recipient.

guide.intro: POR and PARA both translate to 'for' in English, but they mean very different things. Por looks back at causes and reasons; para looks forward to goals and destinations. Getting them right is one of the biggest jumps from A2 to B1.

rows: El informe es para el lunes.

sections.text: POR — cause, duration, exchange, motion through

rows: I did it for/because of love.
I'll work for you (in your place) today.

rows.translation: I work FOR Google. (My employer is Google.)
I'm working in PLACE of Juan.
I bought flowers FOR my mother. (The recipient.)
I bought flowers BECAUSE OF my mother. (My motivation.)

sections.text: Quick test: if you could say 'in order to' in English → PARA. If you could say 'because of' or 'through' → POR.
'Gracias por' (Thanks FOR / because of), 'pagar por' (pay FOR / in exchange), 'ir por' (go to fetch), 'por favor' (please) — fixed expressions worth memorizing.

topics.title: Direct & Indirect Object Pronouns
topics.description: me/te/lo/la/le and the famous 'se lo digo'

guide.intro: Spanish replaces noun objects with short pronouns. You already know some (me, te). At B1 we master DOUBLE pronouns: 'Se lo dije' = 'I told it to him/her'. The order is fixed (indirect + direct), and when both are third person, the indirect 'le/les' shape-shifts to 'se'.

sections.text: When you use both, the indirect always goes first. 'Me lo das' = 'You give it to me.' (me = to me, lo = it).
If BOTH pronouns are third-person (le/les + lo/la/los/las), the indirect 'le' or 'les' becomes 'SE' to avoid the awkward 'le lo'.

rows.translation: I gave it (fem.) to María as a gift.

sections.text: Object pronouns go BEFORE conjugated verbs and AFTER (attached to) infinitives, gerunds, and affirmative commands.

rows.translation: I'm going to tell you. (attached to infinitive)

topics.title: Modals: poder, deber, tener que, hay que

guide.intro: Spanish modal verbs let you talk about possibility, obligation, and necessity. Unlike English ('can / must / should'), Spanish modals conjugate fully and combine with an infinitive: 'puedo ir' (I can go), 'tengo que estudiar' (I have to study).

sections.text: To make modals polite or softer, use the conditional form. 'Puedes' becomes 'podrías' (could you), 'debes' becomes 'deberías' (should — softer).
'Hay que' is IMPERSONAL — it's true for everyone, no specific subject. 'Tener que' is personal — someone specific has to do it.

sections.text: Spanish has NO direct 'must' for inference like English ('he must be tired'). Use 'deber de': 'Debe de estar cansado' = 'He must be tired (probably).' Native speakers often skip the 'de' in casual speech.

topics.title: Storytelling — preterite + imperfect + past perfect
topics.description: Telling a story in past: actions, scenes, and what had happened before

guide.intro: Spanish past tenses split work three ways: PRETERITE for completed actions (what HAPPENED next), IMPERFECT for description and ongoing context (what WAS GOING ON), and PAST PERFECT for things that HAD ALREADY HAPPENED before the story moment. Mastering this trio is what makes you sound natural in narrative.

rows.translation: It was night and it was raining.

rows.source: Yo tenía 12 años. Vivíamos en Madrid.
rows.translation: I was 12. We were living in Madrid.

rows.source: Mi abuela siempre cocinaba los domingos.
rows.translation: My grandma always cooked on Sundays.

rows.source: Llegué a casa a las ocho.

sections.text: Imperfect SETS THE SCENE; preterite PUSHES THE STORY FORWARD. 'Estaba en casa cuando llamó' = 'I was at home (background) when she called (event)'.

rows.source: Cuando era niño, vivía en Barcelona.
rows.translation: When I was a kid (background), I lived in Barcelona.
I was eating when the phone rang.

rows.source: Hacía sol, así que decidimos ir a la playa.
rows.translation: It was sunny, so we decided to go to the beach.

sections.text: Past perfect — what HAD happened first
Use había + participle for an action that happened BEFORE the main story moment.

rows.translation: When I arrived, they had already had dinner.

rows.source: No reconocí la calle: habían construido un edificio nuevo.
rows.translation: I didn't recognize the street: they had built a new building.
I had never seen so much snow.

sections.text: Time markers that often signal IMPERFECT: 'mientras' (while), 'siempre' (always), 'todos los días' (every day), 'a menudo' (often), 'de niño' (as a kid). Markers for PRETERITE: 'ayer', 'el otro día', 'el año pasado', 'en 1990', 'una vez', 'de repente' (suddenly).

Spanish does NOT use the past perfect as freely as English. 'I had eaten when she arrived' usually maps fine to 'Había comido cuando llegó.' But 'I just ate' = 'Acabo de comer' (no past perfect needed).

topics.title: B1 Mixed Review
topics.description: Everything — subjunctive, conditional, ser/estar, por/para, pronouns

guide.intro: Quick refresher of the B1 toolkit. The exercises below mix everything: present perfect, subjunctive triggers, conditional politeness, ser/estar nuance, por/para, double object pronouns, modals, and past-tense storytelling. A great way to spot what still needs work.

rows: he/has + participio — recent past with present link
Permanent label vs current state; some adjectives shift meaning
Imperfect = scene, Preterite = event, Pluscuamperfecto = earlier

rows.source: *Es importante estudias → Es importante que estudies.
*Por mí, es difícil → Para mí, es difícil.
*El café es frío (when it shouldn't be) → El café está frío.

sections.text: When you're unsure, try replacing with the English clue: 'in order to' = para. 'because of / through' = por. 'I want him to...' = querer que + subjunctive. 'Would' = conditional.
